newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels, Fujimori representatives to meet in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Rebels, Fujimori representatives to meet in Peru.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori said on Sunday his chief negotiator in the hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's home, Domingo Palermo, would meet the Marxist rebel chief's deputy in preliminary talks on Tuesday.

Peru's president said on a visit to London the negotiator for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), who are holding 72 hostages in the 54-day-old siege in Lima, would not be rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini but his deputy, known by his nom de guerre "El Arabe" -- "The Arab."
"At this preliminary stage, it is Cerpa Cartolino's number two who will be the interlocutor of Minister Palermo," Fujimori told Peruvian reporters accompanying him on the London visit.
"We hope the preliminary talks will make enough progress to enter definitive talks, probably with Cerpa Cartolini himself," said Fujimori, in a report on Peruvian radio.
The MRTA and government have not held face-to-face talks since Dec. 28, when Education Minister Palermo met Cerpa.
That was 11 days after about 15 heavily-armed MRTA rebels stormed the Japanese envoy's residence and seized hundreds of guests attending an embassy cocktail party.

Most of them have been freed, but the rebels are holding on to their most prized captives, including the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, Peruvian government ministers, Japanese and local businessmen, and Fujimori's brother, Pedro.
The rebels' main demand is the release of about 400 jailed comrades -- something that Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, refuses to discuss.

But the Peruvian president has promised Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to seek a peaceful outcome and he told Reuters in an interview in London: "We will exhaust all possible avenues to ensure that the hostages are freed without the use of force."

Hopes that dialogue would resume were raised by a visit to the residence on Thursday by Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and two other negotiators. Cipriani was back in the building for long visits over the weekend.

While concerns have grown in Lima for the health of the hostages, some of whom are said by relatives to need outside attention despite medical visits organised by the Red Cross, preparations have been quietly going on for new talks.

"The place is already defined; it's a place rented by the Peruvian government under the jurisdiction of the International Red Cross with the participation of the guarantor countries (Japan and Canada) and the Vatican," Fujimori told reporters.
He also referred to the vehicle that will transfer the MRTA negotiator to the talks -- a metallic-blue Chevrolet van.
"We hope that these talks will advance on what have been informal talks and that there can be progress towards getting the liberation of the hostages," said Fujimori.

Peruvian newspaper La Republica on Sunday identified Cerpa's lieutenant "El Arabe" as 34-year-old former bus conductor Roli Rojas. It said Rojas, from a poor family, put himself through university and began guerrilla activities in 1985. Captured in 1986 after an attack on the U.S. ambassador's residence, he was sentenced to 10 years in jail -- but tunneled out in 1990.
Former captives at the residence believed him to be "open to dialogue, likeable, less impetuous than his leader," the newspaper said.
